1. ste80-humanizer

2. simpleenglish
用飞机维修手册用了四十年的受控英语写文档：短句、单义、主动语态

先定配色、字阶、间距，再写组件；目标是让你一眼看不出这是 AI 做的界面
https://colaskill.com/zh/ui-design/

4. styleseed
把设计决定编译成规则文件，渲染完再打分；同一句提示，不会每次长出不同的脸
https://colaskill.com/zh/styleseed/

5. logo-design-skill
从简报、图形策略到 16px、单色、反白测试；附 1400+ 真标志库，但只准研究不准抄
https://colaskill.com/zh/logo-design-skill/

36 种构图按影片情绪挑，中文字体按题材选宋体、黑体、手写或书法，不默认书法

Lemo-opuscar已经突破20Kstar了，今天正好是项目发布整2周的时间，【99个风格】加上【改变风格】玩法让这个库有了可多的可玩性和实用性。项目中不单单能提供风格参考，也给了很多实用的工具用来制作视频。

感谢所有朋友的支持，以及对项目提出issue和PR的contributors。下面这个影片是20K🌟的感谢视频。

未来会继续更新，2.1版本正在计划中。

I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton of public data and 7 hours and 45K lines of code later... it works :)

- 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC...
- Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid.
- The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc.
- 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map.
- Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry
- Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode.

It's deployed here: https://karpathy.ai/usaciv/ and the "?" has the source link too. I don't exactly know where I was going with this but it's really fun to browse and play with. Possibly it can be expanded or built into a game. I only have half of my weekly Claude quote left though so someone else will have to take over :D. Claude also made a trailer:

quoted_tweet.author: Robert Youssef
quoted_tweet.text:
"research clipping" just dropped

https://www.alphaxiv.org/

40-page papers now come as 2-minute videos.

AlphaXiv has started attaching short explainer videos to the papers in its trending section. They're generated with GLM-5.4 and styled after 3Blue1Brown, the YouTuber known for animated lectures on math and neural networks.

You give it a raw arXiv PDF. The model pulls out the key ideas, proposes a visual explanation for each, and renders the whole thing with animation and voiceover.

I watched one on a vision-language paper. It asks which part of a vision encoder actually matters: the pretraining prior, the dedicated capacity, or its placement before fusion with text.

In about two minutes it gets through the findings 👇
→ a from-scratch encoder performs on par with a pretrained one
→ dropping the encoder cuts visual question answering from 44.4 to 39, while text holds
→ moving those parameters into the backbone's first eight layers as vision-only branches matches the encoder
→ encoder-free needs about 4x the compute to catch up
→ with no encoder running first, time to first token drops 13%

It even explains the mechanism. An indicator is set to one for vision tokens and zero for text, so words never touch the new weights, and those weights start at zero.

That's a dense ablation study, compressed into something you can follow on your phone.

The videos sit next to the papers in AlphaXiv's trending section.

text:
We went through 17 small business AI cases that owners published under their own names. Here is what each one handed the AI, and what came back.

> HireEffect, a Dallas bookkeeping and payroll firm, gave it two and a half years of a client's PayPal transactions. It isolated the 16 transactions behind a $13,000 gap.

> Bama Sea Products gave it 20 years of quality data and asked where problems came from, by supplier, product and season. 18 hours later it had a plan for each supplier.

> At Bambi Baby, COO Josh Weiss, who is not a developer, built a scan-to-wishlist tool for walk-in shoppers. $60,000 in sales tied back to it in its first four days.

> KANE, a Princeton agency, feeds it meeting notes and its own past project prices. Getting from a yes to a statement of work out for signature used to take weeks. Now it takes minutes.

> Patrick Schaber runs a task every day at 8am that reads his HubSpot call notes and drafts the follow-ups. That used to take him 30 to 45 minutes a day.

> Tony Severino, a painting contractor near Chicago, caught it pricing a bid with a floor-area multiplier instead of real wall measurements. Now he asks it to "show me your work."

The one that went badly: Karen Spinner's 100+ receipts stalled in Claude Cowork on timeouts and tool call limits. She gave the same job to Claude Code, and it finished in five minutes.

What the 16 wins had in common:

1. They started from their own records.
2. They gave the AI one narrow job.
3. They built in a check before anything went out.

The video walks through every case, plus five free prompts built on those three habits, from a pricing review to churn warning signs.

follow @godofprompt if you run a small business. we break down the AI cases that came with real numbers, and the prompts behind them.

Every message you send in a long Claude chat makes it reread the whole chat. That's where your weekly limit goes.

A post about cutting Claude's token use got 3,000+ bookmarks this week. People feel the limit. Most never change the habits that burn it.

What actually eats your usage:
→ One chat that runs for days. Message 80 carries messages 1 to 79 with it
→ Five short questions sent one by one instead of in one message
→ "Rewrite the whole thing" when you only wanted one paragraph changed
→ The same file pasted again in every new chat

3 prompts that fix the expensive habits:

Prompt 1: The handoff
"This chat is getting long. Write a handoff note for a fresh chat: the goal, decisions we made, facts I gave you, open questions and the next step. Under 200 words, no commentary. I'll paste it as the first message of a new chat."

Prompt 2: Batch it
"I have [5] questions. Answer all of them in one reply, in order, numbered. Keep each answer under 80 words unless the question needs code. If one answer depends on another, say so instead of repeating it."

Prompt 3: Change only what changed
"Don't rewrite the whole document. Show only the paragraphs you'd change, as before and after, and leave everything else out. If nothing needs changing in a section, skip it."

Start a new chat when the topic changes. Keep files you reuse in a Project instead of pasting them every time.

Our free guide has the rest of the playbook: which model for which task, how to keep long work cheap, and the settings that cost you most. Link in the first reply.

You can have Claude pull free public data and turn it into a map of your own market. Karpathy did it with 31 sources and 45,000 lines of code. Your version takes one evening.

Andrej Karpathy asked Claude to fill a Civilization-style map of the US with real data. 7 hours later it had Census numbers, jobs, power plants, ports, parks and disasters on one hex grid. Over a million people have seen it.

The game is the fun part. The useful part: governments publish free data on almost any question you have about your market, and almost nobody looks at it.

The small version for your business:

Prompt 1: Find the data
"My question: [e.g. which 3 neighborhoods in my city need a dog groomer most]. List the free public datasets that could answer it: census, labor statistics, business registries, city open data. For each one: who publishes it, what it covers, how fresh it is, and the link. Rank them by how directly they answer my question. Skip anything behind a paywall or login."

Prompt 2: One table
"Read the top 3 sources [or: here are the files]. Put them in one table by [zip code / city / county]. Flag every row where the sources disagree or data is missing instead of filling the gap. Show me the table and the 3 biggest data problems."

Prompt 3: So what
"From this table, give me 3 conclusions that would change a decision I'm making about [decision]. For each one: the number behind it, how confident you are, and what data would prove you wrong."

In a chat with web search it finds the sources. In Claude Code or Codex it can download and join them for you.

You don't need 45,000 lines of code. You need one good question and data that's already free.
